foodDescription: Grilled chicken tikka in a creamy, mildly spiced tomato sauce. Glasgow’s claim: in the early 1970s Ali Ahmed Aslam at the Shish Mahal restaurant improvised the sauce, tomato soup included, for a diner who found his chicken dry. London disputes it.

A pizza box filled with whatever the takeaway has: doner meat, chicken pakora, chips, onion rings, garlic bread, naan, salad and several sauces, all piled together. Bought late at night from Glasgow’s Indian and Pakistani takeaways, and meant for sharing.

A cheese and tomato pizza, usually halved, dipped in fish batter and deep-fried until the crust crackles and the cheese runs. A Glasgow chip shop staple, ordered as a supper with chips. Eat it standing up, quickly, while the batter is still crisp.

Haggis, the peppery Scottish pudding of sheep’s offal and oats, broken into pieces, dipped in spiced chickpea batter and fried. A Glasgow curry-house starter that joins the city’s two food traditions. Served with a sweet red chilli dip or mint yogurt.

A Glasgow morning roll, floury and soft with a crust that shatters, split and filled with a slice of square sausage, also called Lorne. The local hangover breakfast. Add a fried egg or tattie scone, and choose red sauce or brown — people do care.

Mashed potato kneaded with flour and butter, rolled thin, cut into triangles and cooked dry on a griddle. Fried again in the pan for a Scottish breakfast, or folded into a roll with square sausage. Supermarkets sell them in packs; bakeries’ are better.

Macaroni cheese baked inside a hot-water pastry case, sometimes browned on top under extra cheddar. Carbohydrate inside carbohydrate, sold warm in Glasgow bakeries and at football grounds. Locals eat them cold too, straight from the paper bag.

A Scotch pie of spiced mutton or beef, eaten with a cup of Bovril — a hot, salty beef-extract drink — at half time on the terraces. The standard winter ritual at Celtic Park, Ibrox and Hampden. Hold the pie upright or the grease goes everywhere.

Haddock, not cod, in batter with chips, wrapped and eaten hot. In Glasgow a supper means it comes with chips; a single fish means without. Many of the city’s chip shops were opened by Italian immigrant families, and some still are. Salt and vinegar on top.

Minced beef stewed slowly with onion and carrot until it turns into thick gravy, served with plain boiled or mashed potatoes. The everyday Glasgow dinner for generations. Unglamorous, comforting, and still on the menu in old-fashioned cafés.

A spiced fruit pudding of flour, suet, dried fruit and treacle, wrapped in a cloth — a cloot — and boiled for hours until it forms a dark, shiny skin. Sliced and eaten with custard, or fried for breakfast the next morning. Made at Christmas and birthdays.

A round shortbread biscuit topped with a dome of soft white marshmallow and coated in thin milk chocolate, in red and silver foil. Made by Tunnock’s in Uddingston, east of the city, since 1956. Giant dancing versions opened the 2014 Commonwealth Games.

Glasgow’s word for an ice cream cone, sold from ice cream vans and from the cafés opened by Italian families who arrived from the late 1800s. Vanilla is standard. Ask for a ninety-nine and you get a chocolate flake pushed in the top.

A bright orange fizzy drink made by AG Barr, a Glasgow firm, since 1901, now produced in Cumbernauld. Sweet, faintly of bubblegum and citrus, with a secret recipe. Scots drink it as a hangover cure. A Glaswegian may call any fizzy drink ginger.

A pale, crisp lager brewed at the Wellpark Brewery in the city’s East End, beside the Necropolis cemetery, where Tennent’s began making lager in 1885. The default pint in almost every Glasgow pub. Ask for a pint of Tennent’s and nobody will ask which size.
